lessons.title: Constructions and loci
lessons.summary: Use a ruler and compasses to construct triangles, perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors and perpendiculars, and use these constructions to draw loci and solve problems about regions.
objectives: I can construct a triangle accurately from given side lengths using compasses.
I can construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment and the bisector of an angle.
I can construct a perpendicular from a point to a line and at a point on a line.
I can draw the locus of points a fixed distance from a point or a line, or equidistant from two points or two lines.
I can combine loci to identify a region satisfying several conditions, including on scale drawings.

activities.title: Constructing triangles
activities.content:
## Ruler and compasses only

A **construction** is an accurate drawing made with a ruler (for straight lines), a pair of compasses (for arcs) and, when angles are given, a protractor. The examiner looks for your **construction arcs**: never rub them out, because they are the evidence that you used the correct method.

## A triangle from three sides (SSS)

To construct a triangle with sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm:

1. Draw the longest side, 7 cm, as the base with a ruler. Label the ends A and B.
2. Open the compasses to 5 cm, put the point on A and draw an arc above the base.
3. Open the compasses to 4 cm, put the point on B and draw a second arc crossing the first.
4. Label the crossing point C and join AC and BC.

The arcs must cross clearly. If they do not, the triangle is impossible (two sides shorter than the third cannot meet).

## Other triangles

- **Two sides and the included angle (SAS)**: draw one side, measure the angle at one end with a protractor, draw the second side along that line, join up.
- **Two angles and a side (ASA)**: draw the side, measure both angles at its ends, extend the lines until they meet.

## Accuracy

Exam tolerance is usually ±2 mm on lengths and ±2° on angles. Use a sharp pencil, hold the compasses at the top, and check your lengths after drawing.

question.text: Put the steps in order to construct a triangle with sides 8 cm, 6 cm and 5 cm.
question.hint: Start with the longest side as a base.
question.explanation: Draw the 8 cm base, arc 6 cm from one end, arc 5 cm from the other end, join the crossing point to both ends.
order: Draw the 8 cm base with a ruler and label the ends A and B
Set the compasses to 6 cm and draw an arc from A
Set the compasses to 5 cm and draw an arc from B crossing the first arc
Join the crossing point to A and to B

activities.title: Bisectors
activities.content:
## Perpendicular bisector of a line segment

This is the line that cuts a segment AB exactly in half at right angles. Every point on it is the **same distance from A as from B**.

1. Open the compasses to **more than half** the length of AB.
2. With the point on A, draw arcs above and below the line.
3. Keeping the **same radius**, with the point on B, draw arcs crossing the first two.
4. Join the two crossing points with a ruler. This line is the perpendicular bisector.

If the radius is too small the arcs will not meet; if you change the radius between A and B the line will not pass through the midpoint.

## Angle bisector

This line splits an angle into two equal halves. Every point on it is the **same distance from both arms** of the angle.

1. Put the compass point on the vertex of the angle and draw an arc that crosses both arms.
2. From each crossing point, with the same radius, draw an arc inside the angle. The two arcs cross.
3. Join the vertex to the crossing point.

## Why the arcs matter

The crossings come from equal radii, which is what guarantees equal distances. Measuring with a protractor and marking half the angle is **not** a construction and scores no marks in a "construct" question.

question.text: When constructing the perpendicular bisector of a line segment AB, how wide should the compasses be opened?
question.hint: The arcs from A and from B must cross each other.
question.explanation: The radius must be more than half of AB so that the arcs from each end overlap and cross above and below the line. The same radius must be used from both ends.

options.text: More than half the length of AB, the same from both ends
Exactly half the length of AB
options.feedback: The arcs would only just touch at the midpoint and give no crossing points.

options.text: Less than half the length of AB
Any width, as long as it is different from each end

activities.title: Worked example: perpendiculars
activities.content:
## Perpendicular from a point to a line

Point P sits above a line. To construct the perpendicular from P to the line:

1. Put the compass point on P and draw an arc that crosses the line at **two** points, X and Y.
2. From X and from Y, with the same radius, draw arcs below the line that cross each other at Z.
3. Join P to Z. This line is perpendicular to the original line, and the point where it meets the line is the closest point on the line to P.

The distance from P along this perpendicular is the **shortest distance** from P to the line, which is what "distance from a line" always means.

## Perpendicular at a point on a line

Point Q lies on the line. To construct a right angle at Q:

1. With the compass point on Q, draw arcs crossing the line either side of Q, at X and Y. Now Q is the midpoint of XY.
2. Widen the compasses and construct the perpendicular bisector of XY as before.
3. The bisector passes through Q at right angles to the line.

## Constructing a 60° angle

Draw a line, put the compass point on one end A and draw an arc crossing the line at B. With the point on B and the **same radius**, draw an arc crossing the first arc at C. Angle CAB is exactly 60° because triangle ABC is equilateral. Bisecting it gives 30°; bisecting a right angle gives 45°.

question.text: Match each construction to the first step used to make it.
question.hint: Think about where the compass point goes first.
question.explanation: Perpendicular bisector: arcs from both ends of the segment. Angle bisector: an arc from the vertex across both arms. Perpendicular from a point: an arc from the point crossing the line twice. 60° angle: an arc from one end of a line, then the same radius from where it crosses.

pairs.right: Arcs of equal radius from A and from B, above and below the line
An arc centred on the vertex crossing both arms

pairs.left: Perpendicular from a point P to a line
pairs.right: An arc centred on P crossing the line at two points
An arc from A crossing the line, then the same radius from that crossing

activities.title: Loci
activities.content:
## The path of a moving point

A **locus** (plural **loci**) is the set of all points that obey a rule. There are four standard loci, and each matches a construction you already know.

| Rule | Locus | How to draw it |
|---|---|---|
| a fixed distance $r$ from a point A | a **circle** centre A, radius $r$ | compasses |
| a fixed distance $r$ from a straight line | two **parallel lines** $r$ either side; if the line is a segment, add **semicircles** at the ends to make a rounded "running track" shape | ruler and compasses |
| equidistant from two points A and B | the **perpendicular bisector** of AB | construction |
| equidistant from two lines that meet | the **angle bisector** | construction |

## Regions

Questions often say "less than 3 cm from A" (inside the circle) or "closer to A than to B" (the side of the perpendicular bisector containing A). Shade the region and make it clear which side you mean.

**Boundaries**: "less than" excludes the boundary; "at most" or "no more than" includes it. In practice, draw the boundary and shade the correct side.

## Scale drawings

On a map with scale 1 cm : 2 km, "within 6 km of the transmitter" is a circle of radius **3 cm**. Convert every real distance to a drawing distance before you pick up the compasses, and state the conversion in your working.

question.text: A goat is tied by a 4 m rope to a post in the middle of a large field. Which describes the region the goat can reach?
question.hint: The goat can be any distance up to 4 m from the post, in any direction.
question.explanation: All points at most 4 m from a fixed point form a circle of radius 4 m, including its inside.

options.text: The inside of a circle of radius 4 m centred on the post
A square of side 4 m centred on the post
A straight line 4 m long through the post
Only the circumference of a circle of radius 4 m
options.feedback: The rope can be slack, so the goat can reach anywhere inside too.

question.text: A map has a scale of 1 cm to 5 km. A mobile mast has a range of 12.5 km. What radius, in cm, should be used to draw the circle showing its range on the map?

metadata.blanksText: The locus of points equidistant from two fixed points A and B is the perpendicular ___ of AB. The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines is the angle ___.

question.hint: Both are constructions you make with compasses.
question.explanation: Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector. Equidistant from two lines: the angle bisector.

activities.title: Combining loci and common mistakes
activities.content:
## Regions with more than one condition

A typical problem: a rectangular garden ABCD is drawn to scale. A tree must be planted **more than 2 m from wall AB** and **nearer to corner A than to corner D**.

1. Draw the locus for each condition separately: a line parallel to AB, 2 m (scaled) into the garden; and the perpendicular bisector of AD.
2. Decide which side of each boundary is allowed.
3. Shade the **overlap** where every condition holds.

Label the region clearly, or the examiner may not know which part is your answer.

## Watch out for

- **Rubbing out arcs.** Construction marks are the method; without them you lose marks.
- **Changing the compass radius** part way through a bisector construction.
- **Using a protractor** when the question says "construct".
- **Forgetting the semicircular ends** on the locus around a line segment.
- **Wrong side shaded.** "Closer to A" means the side containing A.
- **Not converting scale.** 3 km on a 1 cm : 2 km map is 1.5 cm.
- **Circle vs disc.** "Exactly 3 cm from P" is the circumference only; "within 3 cm" is the whole disc.
- **Blunt pencils and thick lines** cost accuracy marks. Keep lines thin and arcs light but visible.

question.text:
A rectangular field PQRS is drawn to a scale of 1 cm to 10 m. PQ is 8 cm long and QR is 5 cm long. A water trough is to be placed so that it is:

- at least 20 m from corner P, and
- closer to side PQ than to side SR.

Describe fully the constructions you would draw, including the compass radius, and describe the region where the trough can go.
question.hint: Convert 20 m to cm on the drawing. "Closer to PQ than to SR" means the half of the rectangle nearer PQ; its boundary is the line midway between them.
question.explanation: 20 m = 2 cm. Draw a circle (arc) of radius 2 cm centred on P; the trough must be outside it. Draw the line parallel to PQ and SR midway between them (2.5 cm from each, which is the perpendicular bisector of PS or QR); the trough must be on the PQ side. The region is the part of the rectangle on the PQ side of the midline and outside the 2 cm arc around P.

markScheme.criterion: Converts 20 m to 2 cm using the scale
Arc/circle centred on P of radius 2 cm, with the region outside it
Line parallel to PQ midway between PQ and SR (perpendicular bisector of PS, 2.5 cm from each side)
Region is on the PQ side of the midline and outside the arc

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Constructions use ruler and compasses; **leave all arcs visible**.
- **Triangle (SSS)**: base, then arcs from each end with the other two lengths.
- **Perpendicular bisector**: equal arcs from both ends (radius more than half), join the crossings. Locus of points equidistant from two points.
- **Angle bisector**: arc from the vertex, then equal arcs from the crossings. Locus of points equidistant from two lines.
- **Perpendicular from a point**: arc from the point crossing the line twice, then bisect.
- **Loci**: circle around a point; parallel lines with semicircular ends around a segment.
- Convert with the scale first; shade the overlap for combined conditions.

practiceQuestions.text: Which locus describes all the points exactly 3 cm from a fixed point O?
practiceQuestions.hint: Every point is the same distance from O.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Points at a fixed distance from a point form a circle with that point as centre.

options.text: A circle of radius 3 cm centred at O
A straight line 3 cm from O
A square with sides 3 cm
Two parallel lines 3 cm apart

practiceQuestions.text: What does the locus of points that are exactly 2 cm from a line segment AB look like?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the ends of the segment as well as the middle.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Along the segment the locus is two parallel lines 2 cm away; around each end it curves round as a semicircle of radius 2 cm, making a rounded rectangle (stadium) shape.

options.text: Two parallel lines 2 cm either side of AB joined by semicircles of radius 2 cm at each end
A circle of radius 2 cm around the midpoint of AB
Two parallel lines only, with square ends
options.feedback: The ends must be curved: points near A are 2 cm from A in every direction.

options.text: The perpendicular bisector of AB

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: when a question says "construct", you may use a protractor to measure and mark half the angle instead of using compasses.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does the examiner need to see?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. A construction must be done with compasses, and the arcs must be left visible as evidence.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: A plan uses a scale of 1 : 200. A sprinkler waters everything within 6 m. What radius in cm should the circle have on the plan?
Put the steps in order to construct the bisector of angle ABC (vertex at B).
practiceQuestions.explanation: Arc from B across both arms; equal arcs from those crossings inside the angle; join B to where they cross.
order: With the compass point on B, draw an arc crossing BA and BC
From each crossing point, with the same radius, draw an arc inside the angle
Mark the point where these two arcs cross
Draw a straight line from B through that point

practiceQuestions.text: A 60° angle is constructed with compasses and then bisected twice. What is the size of the smallest angle produced, in degrees?
Match each description of a region to the correct construction and shading.
practiceQuestions.hint: Identify the boundary first, then which side.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Closer to A than B: perpendicular bisector of AB, A's side. Within 3 cm of C: inside a circle radius 3 cm at C. Nearer to line L than line M: angle bisector, L's side.

pairs.left: Points closer to A than to B
pairs.right: Perpendicular bisector of AB, shade the side containing A
Circle radius 3 cm centred C, shade the inside

pairs.left: Points nearer to line L than to line M, where L and M meet
pairs.right: Angle bisector of L and M, shade the side containing L

practiceQuestions.text: A triangle is constructed with sides 9 cm, 6 cm and 4 cm. The perpendicular bisector of the 9 cm side is drawn. How far, in cm, is the point where the bisector meets the 9 cm side from either end of that side?
practiceQuestions.hint: The bisector cuts the side exactly in half.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint, $9 \div 2 = 4.5$ cm from each end.

practiceQuestions.text: Ali tries to construct a triangle with sides 10 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. Select **all** the statements that are true.
practiceQuestions.hint: Can arcs of radius 4 cm and 5 cm drawn from the ends of a 10 cm base ever meet?
practiceQuestions.explanation: 4 + 5 = 9, which is less than 10, so the arcs cannot cross and no such triangle exists. The construction fails regardless of how carefully it is drawn.

options.text: The two arcs will not cross
The triangle is impossible because 4 + 5 < 10
The triangle can be drawn if the 4 cm side is used as the base
options.feedback: Changing the base does not change the side lengths; it is still impossible.

options.text: The construction will work with a sharper pencil

practiceQuestions.text: Describe how to construct, using ruler and compasses only, the perpendicular from a point P to a line that does not pass through P.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start with an arc centred on P.
practiceQuestions.explanation: With the compass point on P, draw an arc crossing the line at two points. From each of these points, with equal radius, draw arcs on the far side of the line so they cross. Join P to the crossing point; this line is perpendicular to the original line.

markScheme.criterion: Arc centred on P crossing the line at two points
Equal arcs from those two points crossing each other, then join P to the crossing point

practiceQuestions.text: Two towns, A and B, are 12 km apart. A new hospital must be built so that it is nearer to A than to B and no more than 8 km from B. On a map with scale 1 cm to 2 km, describe the constructions needed and the region where the hospital can be built.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two conditions, two loci. Convert 8 km and 12 km to map distances.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mark A and B 6 cm apart. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB; the hospital must be on A's side. Draw a circle of radius 4 cm centred on B; the hospital must be inside it. The region is the part of the circle on A's side of the bisector.

markScheme.criterion: Perpendicular bisector of AB constructed, region on A's side
Circle centred on B with radius 4 cm (8 km scaled)
Region is inside the circle and on A's side of the bisector (the overlap)
